title: Reading one line of his
hookLine: pick one line of the Tenth Guru and live with it for a day

lines: A TUNE THAT STAYS ALL DAY.
NOT THE WHOLE BOOK. ONE LINE.
cards: A tune heard once at breakfast can still be playing in your head at dinner. Nobody learned it on purpose. It was short enough to stay, and by evening it had been everywhere you went.

Sikh life has a version of this. In a gurdwara, the morning's hukamnama, one hymn read from the Guru Granth Sahib, is carried home by some Sikhs as the word for the day. Today, try that with the Tenth Guru.
Not his whole book. One line.

teach.h: ONE HUMAN RACE: A LINE FOR CROWDS.
teach.b: Here are three lines from his writings, met along the way, each paraphrased. The first is from the Akal Ustat: recognize the whole human race as one.

That's a line for a crowded train, for the person you'd rather not sit next to. Live with it for a day and every face becomes a test of it. The second comes from the morning swayyas, which sit in the same work.

teach.h: ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.
teach.b: The Guru says: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. That's a line about the heart under the ritual.
Live with it and you start asking where love actually went in what you did. The third is from the Bachitar Natak, about himself.

teach.h: ONLY THE SERVANT: A LINE FOR PRIDE.
teach.b: Whoever calls me God, he warns, will fall; I am only the servant of the Supreme. A line about humility, from someone with every reason to be proud. Live with it and watch how often you'd like a little credit.
Why only one? Because a line has to be carried to be read. Read a whole page and it stays on the page.

teach.h: CARRY ONE, AND IT READS YOU BACK.
teach.b: Carry one line and it starts reading you back, at the sink, in a meeting, in a mood. That fits a habit in Sikh life: the word isn't finished when the book closes.
One line, one day, is enough to find out what the Tenth Guru's words do when they leave the page.

how: Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama from the gurdwara as the word for the day, and some take a line from the Nitnem, including the Tenth Guru's compositions, to recall through the day.

games.q: what does “reading one line of his” mean?
o: reading the Tenth Guru's whole book in one sitting
carrying a single line of his writing all day
copying out his writings by hand as a practice

p: recognize the human race as one
only those who loved found the Lord
only the servant of the Supreme
a hymn carried as the day's word

s: the way to read his writings is to read the whole book at once
today's way is one line, carried for a day, so it leaves the page.
in the Bachitar Natak, the Guru warns against calling him God
whoever calls him God will fall, he says; he is only the servant of the Supreme.
the swayyas line says ritual is how the Lord is found
it says only those who have loved have found the Lord.

games.q: you've read three lines of the Tenth Guru. which should you carry through today?
o: the one that pricks a little.
the one that sounds best out loud.
games.why: one line, the one that catches, carried long enough that it starts reading you back.

practice: Let the three pass by again, one human race, only those who loved, only the servant, and choose the one that pricks a little, not the one you think is best.
Say it slowly in your head, half on the in-breath, half on the out, and if you pray, let it rest beside the name Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Reading one line of his. Choosing a single line of Guru Gobind Singh's writings and carrying it through a whole day, so the words leave the page. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one line, one day. Three lines offered, and one is enough. Twelve hundred fifty days now.

sources.ref: Akal Ustat 85 (Dasam Granth): recognize all humankind as one, paraphrased
Tav Prasad Swayye (Akal Ustat): only those who have loved have found the Lord, paraphrased
Bachitar Natak 6 (Dasam Granth): whoever calls me God will fall; I am the servant, paraphrased
